-	36.521-1 Annex G.7.9 is replaced by G.5.1 and G.5.2.

### G.5.1	Algorithm to calculate pass and fail probabilities

Following basic assumptions for statistical testing are introduced in this clause:

-	Result of single iteration of test procedure loop obeys Bernoulli distribution with error ratio  $p$ , i.e. the probability that the TE observes expected UE behaviour in single iteration (counted as a success) is  $1-p$  and the probability that the TE doesn't observe expected UE behaviour in single iteration (counted as a fail) is  $p$ .

-	Results of different iterations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d).

-	Early decision concept is applied, i.e., the TE repeats multiple iterations of the test procedure loop. For each iteration the TE records its result (count as a success if the TE observes the expected behavior, count as a fail otherwise) and its index in all iterations. When the i-th fail is observed in  $e_{i}$ -th iteration, the TE compares  $e_{i}$  with corresponding pass limit  $N_{p,i}$  and fail limit  $N_{f,i}$ . The TE shall:

-	terminate the test and decide the DUT passes the test if  $e_{i} > N_{p,i}$

-	terminate the test and decide the DUT fails the test if  $e_{i} \leq N_{f,i}$ ,

-	continue the test and make no decision if  $N_{f,i} < e_{i} \leq N_{p,i}$ .

For a more intuitive understanding, we use the state transition diagram shown in Figure G.5.1-1 to describe the entire process of statistical testing. In Figure 1, X-axis and Y-axis denote the success count and fail count in iterations already executed respectively. And the point with coordinate  $\left（i,j\right）$  (referred as state  $\left(i,j\right)$  thereafter) is used to indicates that the DUT has executed  $i+j$  iterations which includes  $i$  successes and  $j$  fails, where  $i,j \geq 0$ .

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure G.5.1-1: Visualization of early decision statistical testing process. In this example, the TE verdicts that the DUT passes the test after executing 15 iterations of test procedure loop. The results of these 15 iterations are “s”, “f”, “f”, “s”, “s”, “s”, “f”, “s”, “s”, “s”, “f”, “s”, “s” and “s” in order (“s” = “success” and “f” = “fail”)

From Figure G.5.1-1 it’s straightforward to get following observations:

-	The DUT is always in state  $\left(0,0\right)$ at the beginning of statistical test since no iteration is executed at that moment.

-	Assume the DUT is in state  $\left(i,j\right)$  after executing  $i+j$ iterations. Then,

-	if the  $i+j+1$ -th iteration counts a success (with probability  $1-p$ ), the success count shall increase 1 and fail count shall remain unchanged after the  $i+j+1$ -th iteration. As a result, the DUT will be in state  $\left(i+1,j\right)$  after the  $i+j+1$ -th iteration. We call that the DUT moves from state  $\left(i,j\right)$  to state  $\left(i+1,j\right)$ , depicted as moving right by one in the diagram.

-	if the  $i+j+1$ -th iteration counts a fail (with probability  $p$ ), the success count remains unchanged and the fail count increases 1 after the  $i+j+1$ -th iteration. Then the DUT will be in state  $\left(i,j+1\right)$  after the  $i+j+1$ -th iteration. We call that the DUT moves from state  $\left(i,j\right)$  to state  $\left(i,j+1\right)$ , depicted as moving up by one in the diagram.

-	The TE shall evaluate whether pass criteria or fail criteria is satisfied every time the DUT has executed a new iteration, i.e. the DUT moves to a new state. Specifically speaking,

-	If pass criterion is satisfied when DUT is in state  $\left（i,j\right）$ , the TE makes the decision that the DUT passes the test. Correspondingly, state  $\left（i,j\right）$ is referred as a passing state (depicted as green points in Figure G.5.1-1);

-	If fail criterion is satisfied when DUT is in state  $\left（i,j\right）$ , the TE makes the decision that the DUT fails the test. Correspondingly, state  $\left（i,j\right）$ is referred as a failure state (depicted as red points in Figure G.5.1-1).

-	If neither pass criterion nor fail criterion is satisfied when DUT is in state  $\left（i,j\right）$ , the TE makes no decision and continues the test. Correspondingly, state  $\left（i,j\right）$ is referred as a non-decidable state (depicted as hollow points in Figure G.5.1-1).

In this way, the statistical testing is represented as a process in which the DUT starts from state  $\left(0,0\right)$ , moves along certain path in the diagram, and finally stops in certain passing state or failure state.

Obviously, there must be a close relationship between the pass/fail states and the pass/fail limits used for the test. The following two conclusions precisely describes the mapping between pass/fail limits and pass/fail states.

Conclusion 1: The DUT is decided to pass the test if and only if the DUT moves from state  $\left（0,0\right）$  to a state belongs to passing state set  $P=\left\{\left(N_{p,i+1}-i,i\right): i=0,1,2, \cdots \right\}$ .

**Proof** : We prove sufficiency first, and then necessity.

-	Sufficiency: If the DUT is in state  $\left（N_{p,i+1}-i,i\right）$ , it means that the DUT has executed  $N_{p,i+1}$  iterations which includes  $i$  success and  $N_{p,i+1}-i$  fails. Clearly, the TE can only get the i+1-th fail as early as the  $N_{p,i+1}+1$ -th iteration, then we have  $e_{i+1} > N_{p,i+1}$ . This is just the pass criterion when the TE collecting the i+1-th fail.

**-	Necessity** : If the TE verdicts the DUT to pass when it collects the i+1-th fail, following inequations must have been satisfied according to the pass criterion:

$$e_{1} \leq N_{p,1}, e_{2} \leq N_{p,2}, \cdots , e_{i} \leq N_{p,i},e_{i+1} > N_{p,i+1}.$$

The DUT is in state  $\left(e_{i}-i, i\right)$  when the i-th fail happens in the  $e_{i}$ -th iteration. Then the next  $N_{p,i+1}-e_{i}$  iterations after the  $e_{i}$ -th iteration must be counted as success since  $e_{i+1} > N_{p,i+1}$ . Then the DUT will be in state  $\left(N_{p,i+1}-i,i\right)$  after executing these  $N_{p,i+1}-e_{i}$ iterations.

Conclusion 2: The DUT is decided to fail the test if and only if the DUT moves from state  $\left（0,0\right）$  to a state belongs to failure set  $F=\left\{\left(j,i+1\right): N_{f,i}-i < j \leq N_{f,i+1}-\left(i+1\right), i=0,1,2, \cdots \right\}$ , where  $N_{f,0} \triangleq -1$ for sake of simplify.

Proof of conclusion 2 is quite similar as the proof of conclusion 1 and is omitted here. Conclusion 1 and 2 have shown the equivalence between pass/fail limits and pass/fail state sets. As a result, the probability that the DUT pass the test for given error ratio  $p$ , passing state set  $P$  and failure state set  $F$ , denoted as  $P_{p}\left(P,F\right)$ , is given by

$$P_{p}\left(P,F\right)=Prob\left\{DUT moves from state\left(0,0\right) to state \left(i,j\right) which belongs to P\right\}.$$

Furthermore, it’s easy to prove that any path from  $state\left(0,0\right)$  to passing state  $\left(i,j\right)$  won’t pass through any passing state or failure state except the ending state. This is because if the path contains a passing state or failure state  $\left（i^{'},j^{'}\right）$  which is not the ending state, the test will be terminated immediately when the DUT is in state  $\left（i^{'},j^{'}\right）$ . Then  $\left（i^{'},j^{'}\right）$  shall be the ending state, i.e.  $\left（i^{'},j^{'}\right）=\left(i,j\right)$ . This contradicts the assumption that state  $\left（i^{'},j^{'}\right）$  is not the ending state. This also means that two events “DUT moves from state  $(0,0)$  to passing state  $(i,j)$ ” and “DUT moves from state  $(0,0)$  to passing state  $(i^{'},j')$ ” are disjoint if  $\left（i^{'},j^{'}\right） \neq \left(i,j\right)$ . Then we have,

$$P_{p}\left(P,F\right)=\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in P}^{}Prob\left\{DUT moves from state\left(0,0\right) to passing state \left(i,j\right)\right\}=\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in P}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right),$$

where  $T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$  is defined as the transition probability from state  $\left(0,0\right)$  to state  $\left(i,j\right)$ , i.e.

$$T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right) \triangleq Prob\left\{DUT moves from state\left(0,0\right) to state \left(i,j\right)\right\}.$$

Similarly, the probability that the DUT fail the test for given error ratio  $p$ , passing state set  $P$  and failure state set  $F$ , denoted as  $F_{p}\left(P,F\right)$ , is derived as

$$F_{p}\left(P,F\right)=\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in F}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$$

From the discussion above we can observe that the calculation of the  $P_{p}\left(P,F\right)$  and  $F_{p}\left(P,F\right)$  is finally transformed into the calculation of the transition probability  $T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$ . Assuming DUT is in state  $\left(i,j\right)$  after the  $i+j$ -th iteration,  $i,j \geq 0$ . Considering that the  $i+j$ -th iteration can only have two possible results: success or fail, we can derive that the DUT can only be in state  $\left(i-1,j\right)$  or state  $\left(i,j-1\right)$  after executing  $i+j-1$ iterations. Then we have:

$$T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)=Prob\left\{DUT moves from state\left(0,0\right) to state \left(i,j\right), passing \left(i-1,j\right)\right\}+Prob\left\{DUT moves from state\left(0,0\right) to state \left(i,j\right), passing state \left(i,j-1\right)\right\}=Prob\left\{DUT moves from state\left(0,0\right) to \left(i-1,j\right)\right\}Prob\left\{DUT moves from state \left(i-1,j\right) to \left(i,j\right)\right\}+Prob\left\{DUT moves from state\left(0,0\right) to \left(i,j-1\right)\right\}Prob\left\{DUT moves from state \left(i,j-1\right) to \left(i,j\right)\right\}$$

The first equation above holds because the event “DUT moves from state  $(0,0)$  to state  $(i,j)$ , passing state  $(i,j-1)$ ” and event “DUT moves from state  $(0,0)$  to state  $(i,j)$ , passing state  $(i-1,j)$ ” are disjoint. And the second equation above holds because results of different iterations are independent.

Furthermore, we have following obvious observations:

If  $i=0$ , obviously the event “DUT moves from state  $\left(0,0\right)$  to state  $\left(i-1,j\right)$ ” won’t happen since state  $\left(i-1,j\right)$  doesn’t exist in this case. Otherwise, the probability that this event occurs equals to   $T_{\left(i-1,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$ according to the definition of transition probability. Then we have

$$Prob\left\{DUT moves from state\left(0,0\right) to \left(i-1,j\right)\right\}=T_{\left(i-1,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)I_{i > 0},$$

Similarly, we can also derive that

$$Prob\left\{DUT moves from state\left(0,0\right) to \left(i,j-1\right)\right\}=T_{\left(i,j-1\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)I_{j > 0},$$

Where,  $I_{i > 0}$  and  $I_{j > 0}$ are indicator functions,

$$I_{i > 0}=\left\{\begin{matrix}1,&if i > 0\\0,&otherwise\end{matrix}\right., I_{j > 0}=\left\{\begin{matrix}1,&if j > 0\\0,&otherwise\end{matrix}\right.$$

If  $\left(i-1,j\right) \in P \cup F$ , the event “DUT moves from state  $\left(i-1,j\right)$  to state  $\left(i,j\right)$ ” won’t happen since the test will be terminated when DUT reaches state  $\left(i-1,j\right)$ . Otherwise, this event is equivalent to the event “result of the  $\left(i+j\right)$ -th iteration is a success”. Then we have

$$Prob\left\{DUT moves from state \left(i-1,j\right) to \left(i,j\right)\right\}=\left(1-p\right)I_{\left(i-1,j\right) \notin P \cup F}$$

Similarly, we can also derive that

$$Prob\left\{DUT moves from state \left(i,j-1\right) to \left(i,j\right)\right\}=pI_{\left(i,j-1\right) \notin P \cup F}.$$

where,

$$I_{\left(i-1,j\right) \notin P \cup F}=\left\{\begin{matrix}1,&\left(i-1,j\right) \notin P \cup F\\0,&otherwise\end{matrix}\right., I_{\left(i,j-1\right) \notin P \cup F}=\left\{\begin{matrix}1,&if \left(i,j-1\right) \notin P \cup F\\0,&otherwise\end{matrix}\right.$$

Finally, we have shown that following conclusion holds.

Conclusion 3: Transition probability  $T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$ can be calculated by

$$T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)=T_{\left(i-1,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)\left(1-p\right)I_{i > 0}I_{\left(i-1,j\right) \notin P \cup F}+T_{\left(i,j-1\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)pI_{j > 0}I_{\left(i,j-1\right) \notin P \cup F}.$$

The conclusion above shows that  $T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$  can be calculated in a dynamic programming manner: Clearly, we can calculate  $T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$  using the above equation if we know the value of  $T_{\left(i-1,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$  and  $T_{\left(i,j-1\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$ ; For the same reason, we can calculate  $T_{\left(i-1,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$  and  $T_{\left(i,j-1\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$  using the equation above if we know the value of   $T_{\left(i-2,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$ ,  $T_{\left(i-1,j-1\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$  and  $T_{\left(i,j-2\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$ ; Repeating the recursion above, at last all we need to know is only  $T_{\left(0,0\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$ . And we know  $T_{\left(0,0\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)=1$  since UE always is in state  $\left（0,0\right）$ when test starts.

Using the recursion above, we can finally obtain  $T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$  and further  $P_{p}\left(P,F\right)$  and  $F_{p}\left(P,F\right)$  for given  $p$ ,  $P$  and  $F$ .

Assume the limit-risk mapping given in 36.521-1 is still used. Then the customer risk  $R_{c}$  and supplier risk  $R_{s}$  for given passing state set  $P$  and failure state set  $F$  is the probability that baseline bad DUT (error ratio =  $Mp$ , where  $M$  is the bad DUT factor) passes the test and the probability that baseline good DUT (error ratio =  $mp$ , where  $m$ is the bad DUT factor) fails the test respectively. Then we have

$$\begin{matrix}R_{c}=\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in P}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{Mp}\left(P,F\right),&R_{s}=\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in F}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{mp}\left(P,F\right)\end{matrix}.$$

### G.5.2	Method of designing pass/fail limit to approach given risk probability

For given error ratio  $p$ , confidence level  $P_{CL}$ , good DUT factor  $m$  and bad DUT factor  $M$ , pass limit  $\left\{N_{p,i},i=1,2, \cdots \right\}$  and fail limit  $\left\{N_{f,i}:i=1,2, \cdots \right\}$ can be obtained by using the method listed below. Note that the limit-risk mapping in 36.521-1 is assumed.

**Step 1** : Initialize as follows:

- Set  and , passing state set and failure state set respectively, as .
- Set  and , customer risk and supplier risk respectively, as ;
- Set , number of executed iterations, as ;
- Set , non-decidable state set after -th iteration, as ;
- Set  and , transition probability to state  for baseline good DUT and for baseline bad DUT respectively, as , .
- Select  and , step size for customer risk and supplier risk respectively, as , .
![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure G.5.2-1: Demonstration of step 1

Figure G.5.2-1 is the demonstration of step 1. The reason to initialize  $=\left\{\left(0,0\right)\right\}$ ,  $T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{mp}\left(P,F\right)=1$ ,  $T_{\left(0,0\right)}^{Mp}\left(P,F\right)=1$  is because the DUT is always in state  $\left(0,0\right)$  before executing any iteration. And we have  $P, F= \varnothing$ since no passing state or failure state is selected yet.

Step 2: Calculate set  $S^{'}$ , the set of the state can be reached after the n+1-th iteration, as  $S^{'}=\left\{\left(i,j\right):\left(i-1,j\right) \in  S or \left(i,j-1\right) \in S\right\}$ . Then for all state  $\left（i,j\right） \in S^{'}$ , calculate  $T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{Mp}\left(P,F\right)$  and  $T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{mp}\left(P,F\right)$ as follows:

$$T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{Mp}\left(P,F\right)=T_{\left(i-1,j\right)}^{Mp}\left(P,F\right)\left(1-Mp\right)I_{i > 0}I_{\left(i-1,j\right) \notin P \cup F}+T_{\left(i,j-1\right)}^{Mp}\left(P,F\right)MpI_{j > 0}I_{\left(i,j-1\right) \notin P \cup F},$$

$$T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{mp}\left(P,F\right)=T_{\left(i-1,j\right)}^{mp}\left(P,F\right)\left(1-mp\right)I_{i > 0}I_{\left(i-1,j\right) \notin P \cup F}+T_{\left(i,j-1\right)}^{mp}\left(P,F\right)mpI_{j > 0}I_{\left(i,j-1\right) \notin P \cup F}.$$

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure G.5.2-2: Demonstration of step 2

See Figure G.5.2-2 for better understanding of step 2. If DUT doesn’t pass or fail the test after the n-th iteration then DUT must be in one state in  $S$ . It’s easy to observe that the DUT must be in one state in  $S^{'}$ . Then the transition probability to state in  $S^{'}$  can be calculated by using Conclusion 3. For example, the only way to move to state  $D$  in Figure 2 is to first move to state  $A$  then count a fail in the n+1-th iteration, then we have  $T_{D}^{p}=T_{A}^{p}p$ . On the other hand, to move to state  $E,$ the DUT can first move to state  $B$  then count a success in the n+1-th iteration or first move to state  $C$  then count a fail in the n+1-the iteration, i.e.  $T_{E}^{p}=T_{B}^{p}\left(1-p\right)+T_{C}^{p}p.$

Step 3: First, try finding an integer  $n_{e}$  which satisfies  $\left(n+1-n_{e},n_{e}\right) \in S^{'}$ ,  $R_{c}+\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'}\\j \leq n_{e}}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{Mp}\left(P,F\right) \leq 1-P_{CL}$  and  $R_{s}+\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'}\\j > n_{e}}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{mp}\left(P,F\right) \leq 1-P_{CL}$ . If such a  $n_{e}$ exists, let

$$\begin{matrix}R_{c}=R_{c}+\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j \leq n_{e}}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{Mp}\left(P,F\right),&R_{s}=R_{s}+\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j > n_{e}}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{mp}\left(P,F\right),\end{matrix}$$

$$\begin{matrix}P=P \cup \left\{\left(i,j\right):\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j \leq n_{e}\right\}, &F=F \cup \left\{\left(i,j\right):\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j > n_{e}\right\}\end{matrix},$$

If such a  $n_{e}$  doesn’t exist, instead try finding integers  $n_{p}$  and  $n_{f}$ which satisfy

$$\begin{matrix}\left(n+1-n_{p},n_{p}\right) \in S^{'},&\left(n+1-n_{f},n_{f}\right) \in S^{'},\end{matrix}$$

$$\min(\left(i_{c} \Delta _{c},1-P_{CL}\right)) < R_{c}+\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j \leq n_{p}}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{Mp}\left(P,F\right) \leq \min(\left(\left(i_{c}+1\right) \Delta _{c},1-P_{CL}\right)),$$

$$\min(\left(i_{s} \Delta _{s},1-P_{CL}\right)) < R_{s}+\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j \geq n_{f}}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{mp}\left(P,F\right) \leq \min(\left(\left(i_{s}+1\right) \Delta _{s},1-P_{CL}\right)).$$

Then,

-	if such a  $n_{p}$ exists, set

$$R_{c}=R_{c}+\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j \leq n_{p}}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{Mp}\left(P,F\right), P=P \cup \left\{\left(i,j\right):\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j \leq n_{p}\right\}, i_{c}=i_{c}+1.$$

-	if such a  $n_{f}$ exists, set

$$R_{s}=R_{s}+\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j \geq n_{f}}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{mp}\left(P,F\right), F=F \cup \left\{\left(i,j\right):\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j \geq n_{f}\right\}, i_{s}=i_{s}+1.$$

Two possible cases in step 3 are depicted in figure G.5.2-3 and figure G.5.2-4 respectively. If  $n_{e}$  exists, even we add all states  $\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'}$  with  $j \leq n_{e}$  to  $P$  and all states  $\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'}$  with  $j > n_{e}$  to  $F$ , the customer risk and supplier risk are still no larger than  $1-P_{CL}$ (the increment of the customer risk and supplier risk, are denoted as blue and green triangle in figure 4 respectively).

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure G.5.2-3: Demonstration of step 3 ( $n_{e}$ exists)

If  $n_{e}$  doesn’t exist, instead we try to find state set  $\left\{\left(i,j\right):\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j \leq n_{p}\right\}$  which satisfies that the total transition probability to any state in the set is approximately  $\Delta _{c}$ . If such a set exists we can add states in this set to  $P$  without breaking customer risk threshold. Similarly, we can also try to a state set $\left\{\left(i,j\right):\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'},j \geq n_{f}\right\}$  which satisfies that the total transition probability to any state in the set is approximately  $\Delta _{s}$  and add states in this set to  $F$ .

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure G.5.2-4: Demonstration of step 3 ( $n_{e}$ doesn’t exist)

Step 4: Let  $S=S^{'} \text{ \textbackslash } \left(P \cup F\right)$ ,  $n=n+1$ . Then go back to Step 2 if  $S \neq  \varnothing$ , otherwise go to Step 5.

If a state  $\left(i,j\right) \in S^{'}$  is selected as a passing state or failing state then it’s no longer a non-decidable state. Then we need to exclude it from non-decidable state set after n+1-the iteration. If all states in  $S^{'}$ are excluded, clearly the test surely will terminate after the n+1-the iteration and the designing is finished. Otherwise, we need to go back to step 2 and repeat procedures above.

Step 5: Sort all states  $\left(i,j\right)$  in  $P$  in the ascending order of  $j$  and all states  $\left(i,j\right)$  in  $F$  in the ascending order of  $i$ , i.e. we denote

$$P=\left(A_{0},0\right), \left(A_{1},1\right), \left(A_{2},2\right), \left(A_{3},3\right) \cdots , F=\left(0,B_{0}\right), \left(1,B_{1}\right),\left(2,B_{2}\right),\left(3,B_{3}\right), \cdots$$

Then construct passing state set  $P^{'}$  and failure state set  $F^{'}$ as

$$P^{'}=\left\{\left(A_{j}^{'},j\right):j=0,1,2, \cdots \right\}, F^{'}=\left\{\left(i,B_{i}^{'}\right):i=0,1,2 \cdots \right\}$$

Where  $A_{j}^{'}=\min_{k \geq j}A_{k}, B_{i}^{'}=\min_{k \geq i}B_{i}$

Purpose of step 5 is to further optimize the passing state and failure state obtained in step 2 to 4. To understand step 5, we only need to note that all path to passing state  $A,B$  must also pass state  $C,D$ . On the other hand, if a path passes state  $D$  or  $E$ , it must eventually reach one passing state in  $A$ ,  $B$  and  $C$ . Then one can derive that

$$\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in \left\{A,B,C\right\}}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)=\sum_{\left(i,j\right) \in \left\{A,D,E\right\}}^{}T_{\left(i,j\right)}^{p}\left(P,F\right)$$

In other words, if  $P=\left\{A,B,C\right\}$  is a passing set which satisfies customer risk requirements, then  $P^{'}=\left\{A,D,E\right\}$  is also a passing set satisfying customer risk requirements since it has exactly the same customer risk as  $P$ . But  $P^{'}$  is a better choice than  $P$ since it requires fewer iterations to make decision.

For the same reason, we can also derive that failure set  $F^{'}=\left\{F,G,L,M,N,K\right\}$  has same supplier risk with  $F=\left\{F,G,H,I,J,K\right\}$ but requires fewer iterations to fail the test.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure G.5.2-5: Demonstration of step 3 ( $n_{e}$ doesn’t exist).

Step 6: Construct pass limit  $\left\{N_{p,i}\right\}$  and fail limit  $\left\{N_{f,i}\right\}$ as follows:

$$\begin{matrix}N_{f,1}=\max_{B_{i}=1}\left(i+B_{i}\right),&N_{f,2}=\max_{B_{i}=2}\left(i+B_{i}\right),&N_{f,3}=\max_{B_{i}=3}\left(i+B_{i}\right),& \cdots \end{matrix}$$

At last, we can convert pass/fail state sets to pass/fail limits by using conclusion 3 in Annex G.5.1.

###### ServingCellConfig-TxSwitch

## I.1	Direct far field (DFF)

### I.1.1	RX beam peak direction search

The Rx beam peak direction search can be found using any of the following options:

-	Same measurement procedure as in clause Annex K.1.2 of TS 38.521-2 [18].

-	Any of the procedures described in Annex I.4.

### I.1.2	Search for directions corresponding to the EIS spherical coverage percentile

The test directions corresponding to the EIS spherical coverage percentile can be found using any of the following options:

-	EIS spherical coverage scan procedure as described in Annex K.1.6 of TS 38.521-2 [18].

-	Any of the procedures described in Annex I.4.

## I.2	Direct far field (DFF) simplification

### I.2.1	RX beam peak direction search

The Rx beam peak direction search can be found using any of the following options:

-	Same measurement procedure as in clause Annex K.2.2 of TS 38.521-2 [18].

-	Any of the procedures described in Annex I.4.

### I.2.2	Search for directions corresponding to the EIS spherical coverage percentile

The test directions corresponding to the EIS spherical coverage percentile can be found using any of the following options:

-	EIS spherical coverage scan procedure as described in Annex K.1.6 of TS 38.521-2 [18].

-	Any of the procedures described in Annex I.4.

## I.3	Indirect far field (IFF)

### I.3.1	RX beam peak direction search

The Rx beam peak direction search can be found using any of the following options:

-	Any of the procedures described in Annex I.4.

### I.3.2	Search for directions corresponding to the EIS spherical coverage percentile

The test directions corresponding to the EIS spherical coverage percentile can be found using any of the following options:

-	Any of the procedures described in Annex I.4.

Same as in clause I.3.2 for IFF.

## I.4	Procedures to search test directions for RRM FR2

### I.4.1	RSRPB-based scan with fallback option to Rx beam peak direction search

This clause provides RSRPB-based scan to find the Rx beam peak of the UE for Setup 1, single AoA cases and one of the test directions for Setup 4. It also provides a method to find test directions fulfilling the EIS Spherical Coverage (TS 38.521-2 [18] clause 7.3.4.3) for Setup 2, 3 and 4. Other approaches are not precluded. RSRPB-based peak beam scan greatly reduces the time to find the peak beam position compared to traditional EIS scan using either constant step size or constant density. The procedure can be used with DFF as well as IFF methodology. The procedure is achieved implementing the following steps:

1.	Enable periodic RSRPB reporting from the UE

2.	Set of grid points for the UE scan can be user defined set or entire sphere.

3.	Set the DL SSB\_RP (at the centre of the QZ) to -95 dBm / SCS. For each grid point, record RSRPB first by connecting SS to the DUT through the measurement antenna with PolLink=  polarization to form the Rx beam towards the measurement antenna.

4.	Wait for BEAM\_SELECT\_WAIT\_TIME before recording the RSRPB reports.

4a	For each of the grid points, calculate the RSRPB result for PolLink= as the linear sum of the 2 RSRPB reports (one per receiver branch).

4b	Repeat Steps 3, 4 and 4a with PolLink= .

5.	Once the grid points scan is completed, sort the grid points based on the linear sum of the RSRPB results for PolLink= and PolLink= .

6.	For the top 10 grid points, run the REFSENS throughput test as per the test condition defined in TS 38.521-2 [18] clause 7.3.2.

7.	Select the grid point with the best REFSENS result among the 10 points from Step 6 as the Rx beam peak for RRM test cases using AoA Setup 1 or 4.

8.	Use the EIS result for the RRM beam peak to offset the RSRPB results to obtain an estimate of the EIS Spherical coverage (SC) map.

9.	From the EIS map in Step 8, select all the points meeting the EIS SC criteria (as defined in TS 38.521-2 [18] Clause 7.3.4.3) as potential test directions for AoA Setup 2a, 2b, 3 and 4. In order to confirm that the grid point is suitable, run the REFSENS throughput test as per the test condition defined in TS 38.521-2 [18] clause 7.3.2 and verify that the EIS SC criteria is met.

If not enough grid points are found using this method, fallback to using the method in Annex I.1, I.2, I.3 or I.3A as applicable.

## I.5	Re-Positioning Approach for RRM FR2

This clause provides guidance on the applicability of the re-positioning approach which was originally introduced to reduce measurement uncertainties due to positioner blocking as described in Annex N.3 of [18]. Illustrations of the applicability in the following clauses are based on example 1-AoA and 2-AoA capable RRM test systems shown in Figure I.5-1. The probes shown in blue and red are shown for simplicity as typical microwave probes antennas; any of these probes could be implemented as probe&amp;reflector combinations to yield applicable IFF, Enhanced IFF, IFF+DFF test setups, see Clause I.0. The number of locations of the 2 AoA probes are chosen arbitrarily, i.e., systems with fewer and different probe locations are applicable.

<!-- 🖼️❌ Image not available. Please use `PdfPipelineOptions(generate_picture_images=True)` -->

Figure I.5-1: Example combined-axes RRM system setup to support 1 AoA (top) and 1 AoA &amp; 2 AoA test cases (bottom)

The re-positioning approach is applicable to RRM test cases if, during the test case, the pedestal is not obstructing the beam path and it is not in closer proximity to the measurement antenna/reflector than the DUT [18], i.e., for the selected DUT alignment options and orientations only the directions of test (AoA) in the upper hemisphere away from the positioner are tested.

### I.5.1	1 AoA Test Cases

The 1 AoA test cases follow Setups 1 and 2, see Clauses A.9.1 and A.9.2, respectively. Here, the re-positioning approach is applicable only when the pedestal is not obstructing the beam path and that the pedestal is not in closer proximity to the measurement antenna/reflector than the DUT. Therefore, for the selected DUT alignment option and orientation, only the upper hemisphere away from the positioner shall be tested for all the test iterations (if applicable), i.e., the positioner shall always be in the back hemisphere of the 1 AoA probe for each test iteration.

This requirement is illustrated next using the example 1 AoA RRM systems from Figure I.5-1. For the example systems in Figure I.5-1 with P0 (shown in blue) used as active probe, the directions of testing (AoA) within the yellow highlighted upper hemisphere shall be considered so the pedestal is not obstructing the beam path. In this case, the re-positioning approach applies and the optimized QoQZ MU is applicable to the assessed MU of the test system. The different test conditions and orientations from Clause N.2 of [18] can be used for each test iteration to prevent the pedestal from obstructing the beam path.

When the directions of testing (AoA) are outside the yellow highlighted upper hemisphere, i.e. the pedestal is obstructing the beam path, the re-positioning approach no longer applies. In this case, the calculated MU for QoQZ shall include the full range of rotation angles described in the QoQZ procedure, Annex O of [18].

<!-- 🖼️❌ Image not available. Please use `PdfPipelineOptions(generate_picture_images=True)` -->

Figure I.5.1-1: Ranges of possible directions of testing (AoA) for 1 AoA TCs that are applicable with re-positioning concept

### I.5.2	2 AoA Test Cases

The 2 AoA test cases follow Setups 3 and 4, see Clauses A.9.3 and A.9.4, respectively. Here, the re-positioning approach is applicable only when the pedestal is not obstructing the beam paths between each of the 2 active AoA probes and the pedestal is not in closer proximity to the measurement antennas/reflectors than the DUT. Therefore, for the selected DUT alignment option and orientation, the positioner shall always be in the back hemispheres of each of the active AoA probe for each test iteration.

This requirement is illustrated next using the example 2 AoA RRM system from Figure I.5-1. Figure I.5.2-1 shows the acceptable directions of test for the re-positioner concept separately for each active probe. The directions of testing (AoAs) within the respective yellow highlighted upper hemisphere shall be considered so the pedestal is not obstructing any of the beam paths. In this case, the re-positioning approach applies and the optimized QoQZ MU is applicable to the assessed MU of the test system. The different test conditions and orientations from Clause N.2 of TS 38.521-2 [18] can be used for each test iteration to prevent the pedestal from obstructing the beam paths.

When the directions of testing (AoAs) are outside the yellow highlighted upper hemisphere for at least one active probe, i.e., the pedestal is obstructing at least one beam path, the re-positioning approach no longer applies. In this case, the calculated MU for QoQZ shall include the full range of rotation angles described in the QoQZ procedure, Annex O of [18].

<!-- 🖼️❌ Image not available. Please use `PdfPipelineOptions(generate_picture_images=True)` -->

Figure I.5.2-1: Ranges of possible directions of testing (AoAs) for each active probe
